blocks.text: 1. Cross Encoder

blocks.alt: A query and document processed together go through a cross encoder to produce a relevance score

blocks.text: Cross Encoder gives the first previewed technique its own full treatment: the most precise re-ranking approach.
It feeds the query and a candidate chunk into the model together, at the same time, the most accurate re-ranking approach.
2. Processing Both Together
A cross encoder does not embed the query and chunk separately at all.
Both get concatenated and passed through the model as one single input.
3. Why Joint Processing Captures More

blocks.alt: A query and document feed joint attention

blocks.text: As with why retrieval scores aren't always optimal in Why Re-Ranking, a single compressed vector cannot capture every possible interaction between query and chunk.
Processing them together lets the model directly attend to specific word level connections.
4. Outputting A Single Relevance Score

blocks.alt: A cross encoder outputs a single relevance score

blocks.text: Instead of producing a vector, a cross encoder outputs one single relevance number directly.
That number represents exactly how relevant this specific chunk is to this specific query.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Model type","Output"],"rows":[["Bi-encoder, covered next in this module","A vector, compared separately"],["Cross encoder","A single relevance score for this exact pairing"]]}

blocks.text: 5. No Caching Possible

blocks.alt: Each query-document pair must be computed fresh

blocks.text: As with precomputing chunk embeddings in Dense Retrieval, a bi-encoder could precompute chunk embeddings ahead of time.
A cross encoder cannot, since every score depends on the specific query paired with it.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Unlike a bi-encoder's precomputed chunk embeddings, a cross encoder must run its full model computation fresh for every single query and chunk pairing, with no way to reuse prior work.

blocks.text: 6. Computational Cost Per Candidate

blocks.alt: N candidates require N forward passes

blocks.text: Scoring N candidates means running the model N separate times, once per candidate.
As with the cost of the second pass in Why Re-Ranking, that cost is exactly why re-ranking only runs on a small candidate set.
7. Accuracy Versus Scalability Tradeoff

blocks.alt: A cross encoder has high accuracy while a bi-encoder has high scale

blocks.text: Cross encoders produce the most accurate relevance scores among common re-ranking techniques.
That accuracy comes at the cost of being far too slow for first stage retrieval at scale.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running a cross encoder against millions of stored chunks directly would be far too slow for real time search, which is exactly why cross encoders only ever run on the small candidate set retrieval already narrowed down.

blocks.text: 8. Where Cross Encoders Actually Run
As with the two stage pipeline in Why Re-Ranking, cross encoders belong exclusively in the second, re-ranking stage.
Never in the first stage, where broad, fast retrieval happens instead.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pipeline stage","Model type used"],"rows":[["Stage one, first stage retrieval","Bi-encoder, fast and scalable"],["Stage two, re-ranking","Cross encoder, slow but precise"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When A Cross Encoder Is The Right Re-Ranking Choice

blocks.alt: A small candidate set needing high precision points toward a cross encoder

blocks.text: Small candidate sets needing maximum accuracy suit cross encoders well.
Large candidate sets or tight latency budgets need a faster technique, covered later in this module.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates scoring a query and chunk pairing jointly instead of comparing separate embeddings.

code.content:
def fake_cross_encoder_score(query, chunk_text):
    # Simulate joint processing of query and chunk together
    combined_input = f"{query} [SEP] {chunk_text}"
    query_words = set(query.lower().split())
    chunk_words = set(chunk_text.lower().split())
    shared = query_words & chunk_words
    # simulate joint attention by weighting shared word density
    density = len(shared) / max(len(query_words) + len(chunk_words) - len(shared), 1)
    return round(density, 3)

query = "how do I get a refund for a damaged item"
candidates = [
    "Damaged items are eligible for a full refund within thirty days.",
    "Our shipping partners deliver most orders within a week.",
    "Refunds require proof of purchase and are processed in five days.",
]

print(f"Query: {query!r}\n")
print("Cross encoder scores:")
for chunk in candidates:
    score = fake_cross_encoder_score(query, chunk)
    print(f"  {score}: {chunk!r}")

print("\nEach score required a separate full model run.")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows each candidate receiving its own dedicated relevance score computed jointly with the query, rather than comparing precomputed embeddings.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Using a cross encoder for first stage retrieval across an entire large collection.
Assuming cross encoder scores can be precomputed and cached like bi-encoder embeddings.
Ignoring the per candidate computational cost when choosing how many candidates to re-rank.
Skipping a cross encoder for applications where maximum accuracy matters most.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: A cross encoder feeds the query and a candidate chunk into the model together, at the same time.
It does not embed them separately; both get processed as one combined input.
Joint processing lets the model attend directly to specific word level connections between them.
A cross encoder outputs a single relevance score, not a vector, for each specific pairing.
Unlike bi-encoders, cross encoder scores cannot be precomputed or cached ahead of time.
Scoring N candidates requires N separate full model runs, one per candidate.
Cross encoders produce the most accurate relevance scores but are too slow for first stage retrieval.
They belong exclusively in the second, re-ranking stage of a two stage pipeline.
Next up: Bi-Encoder, covering the faster, more scalable alternative used earlier in the pipeline.
